intros.intro:
Imagine an agent that is told how well it did only once in a while, yet is judged on everything it does. Semi-supervised reinforcement learning is the framework Concrete Problems in AI Safety (2016) builds around that setup, its main technical route to oversight that cannot be given constantly.

The prose below explains the fraction-of-episodes setup and then surveys the four concrete approaches the paper sketches for it. After that come the concept's place under scalable oversight, the four approaches it contains, its connections to neighboring ideas, the lens it belongs to, and source links into the paper.

The simplest way to cope with scarce reward is to guess the missing values: train a model to predict reward from what the agent sees, and trust its guesses where no true label exists. Supervised reward learning is the most direct of the four approaches Concrete Problems in AI Safety (2016) offers for its semi-supervised framework.

Two sections follow, one on predicting reward from state and one on this approach's role as the base of its small family. The page then locates the concept under semi-supervised reinforcement learning and lists its two connections, its lens, and its sources in the paper.

Rather than passively accepting whichever episodes happen to be labeled, an agent could ask: it could notice salient events and request reward feedback on those in particular. Concrete Problems in AI Safety (2016) calls this semi-supervised or active reward learning, a refinement of its basic reward-prediction proposal.

Reading down, you will find a section on adding active learning to reward prediction, then one placing the idea among its sibling approaches. Navigation blocks follow: the parent framework it belongs to, its single connection, its lens, and links to the source passages.

Even an episode with no reward attached still shows how the world moves. Unsupervised value iteration, one of four proposals in Concrete Problems in AI Safety (2016), puts those unlabeled transitions to work, using them to sharpen the value estimates an agent keeps through Bellman updates.

The first section explains how updates are made from unlabeled transitions; the second pairs the idea with its companion and its complement among the sibling proposals. Below the prose sit the parent framework, connections to two neighbors, the shared lens, and deep links into the paper.

For an agent that plans with a learned model of its environment, reward-free episodes are still useful: they reveal how states follow from actions. Unsupervised model learning, the fourth of the semi-supervised proposals in Concrete Problems in AI Safety (2016), uses such episodes to improve that dynamics model.

Two short sections follow, one on sharpening a dynamics model without reward and one presenting the idea as the model-based mirror of unsupervised value iteration. Then come the parent framework, a single connection, the shared lens, and source links.

Long before AI safety borrowed the idea, natural language processing researchers were training systems without labeling each example, supplying aggregate statistics or rules that stamp out many noisy labels instead. Distant supervision names that family of techniques, which Concrete Problems in AI Safety (2016) picks up as one route to cheaper oversight.

The sections below describe the trade of per-example evaluation for weaker signal, then follow two branches off scalable oversight. Afterward the page shows where the concept nests and the system it contains, its three connections, its lens, and the source passages.

DeepDive is a working system from Stanford that builds knowledge bases from rules its users write, each rule generating many rough labels at once. Concrete Problems in AI Safety (2016) cites it as proof that this style of weak supervision holds up in practice.

One section describes the rule-based system itself; a second explains why the paper treats it as evidence rather than a technique to adopt. The rest of the page places the concept under distant supervision and notes its single connection, its lens, and where in the paper it appears.

Some agents work like organizations: a top level decides broad, long-horizon moves, and lower levels handle the details in exchange for rewards of their own. Hierarchical reinforcement learning is that longstanding paradigm, which Concrete Problems in AI Safety (2016) revisits because layered delegation might let sparse oversight stretch further.

Below, a section on delegation across timescales precedes one on why the structure promises scalable oversight. Then come the concept's place in the hierarchy, the earlier architecture it contains, its three connections, its lens, and sources.

In 1993, Dayan and Hinton sketched a control scheme run like a fiefdom: manager agents set goals, and worker agents chase synthetic rewards for meeting them. Feudal reinforcement learning is that early architecture, remembered here as the starting point of hierarchical RL.

The prose covers the manager-worker arrangement and its synthetic rewards first, then what the design lends to scalable oversight and the warning that travels with it. Beneath that, the page records the parent paradigm, one connection, its lens, and links into the paper that cites it.

Atari's old video games found a second life as a standard proving ground for reinforcement learning. On this wiki they appear not as a technique but as a testbed: Concrete Problems in AI Safety (2016) borrows them as a toy world for its oversight and reward-hacking experiments.

First the page explains how a pre-existing benchmark was repurposed as a difficulty ladder, then what that enables: a graded test of how little reward feedback an agent can manage on. A single connection, one lens, and source links close the page.

Flip a weighted coin: usually take the best action you know, occasionally take one at random. That simple rule, epsilon-greedy exploration, has guided reinforcement learning agents for decades, and it is entirely indifferent to whether the random action happens to be dangerous.

The page's two sections cover the policy itself, far older than the paper that cites it, and why Concrete Problems in AI Safety (2016) treats it as unsafe by omission. Its parent problem, a single connection, its lens, and sources follow.

Optimism can be a strategy. R-max, an algorithm Brafman and Tennenholtz published in 2003, assumes every unexplored action might yield maximum reward, which provably drives an agent to try everything, dangerous corners included.

Three sections carry the page: the pre-existing algorithm and its near-optimality guarantee, the mechanism of optimism in the face of uncertainty, and why that same mechanism is both the guarantee and the hazard. After the prose come its place under safe exploration, two connections, its lens, and links to the cited passages.

Most reinforcement learning chases the average outcome. A separate body of work asks agents to mind the worst one instead, swapping expected reward for objectives that bound variance or the probability of disaster. Concrete Problems in AI Safety (2016) surveys this literature as risk-sensitive performance criteria.

The page moves through three sections: a body of work the paper imports rather than invents, the mathematics of replacing an expectation with something else, and what these objectives target that a near-optimality proof does not. A parent problem, one connection, one lens, and sources round out the page.

Why let an agent learn by trial and error when someone already knows how the job is done? Using demonstrations means handing the agent expert trajectories to learn from, so risky exploration may not be needed at all; Concrete Problems in AI Safety (2016) proposes it as a remedy for safe exploration.

Three sections follow: learning from experts instead of exploring, the two different jobs one technique performs, and the note that a later paper actually built it. The page then shows its parent and the paradigm it contains, four connections, two lenses, and sources.

Abbeel and Ng showed in 2005 that an agent can reach near-optimal behavior straight from expert trajectories, no trial and error required. Apprenticeship learning is their name for that paradigm, and Concrete Problems in AI Safety (2016) leans on it when arguing that demonstrations can substitute for risky exploration.

From there, the prose covers the technique's history before the paper, its mechanism of matching feature expectations, and why the paper cares about the distinction it draws. The parent remedy, one connection, one lens, and the source citations complete the page.

One way to make dangerous learning safe is to move it somewhere consequence-free. Simulated exploration, a remedy proposed in Concrete Problems in AI Safety (2016), has the agent meet danger inside a simulation first, so that a more cautious policy can be brought out into the real world.

The sections below take the idea in turn: moving exploratory risk into simulation, what the paper admits the move does not solve, and where it sits among the other exploration remedies. This concept has no recorded connections, so the closing blocks are its parent problem, its lens, and sources.

Suppose some region of the world is known to be forgiving, a place where even the worst action can be recovered from. Bounded exploration, proposed in Concrete Problems in AI Safety (2016), lets an agent roam freely inside such a region and uses models to check any step that would leave it.

Down the page: shrinking the space rather than the objective, the worst-case framing borrowed from robust control, and the question of who does the checking and what it needs to get started. The parent problem, three connections, one lens, and source links follow the prose.

Control engineers of the early 1980s built a theory around a pessimistic question: how badly can a bounded disturbance shake a system, and how do you design for that worst case? H-infinity control is that framework, and it enters this wiki because AI safety keeps borrowing its way of thinking.

The two sections contrast worst-case with average-case design, then trace the two safety mechanisms the framework underlies. This concept stands on its own rather than nesting under a problem; below the prose come its two connections, the two lenses it appears in, and sources.

A learner can be chaperoned by a policy that is already trusted: before an exploratory action is taken, the trusted policy and a model of the environment judge whether the agent could recover from it. Concrete Problems in AI Safety (2016) proposes this arrangement as trusted policy oversight.

Three sections develop the idea: delegating the recoverability check to a second policy, one concrete way to run the more abstract check, and the case for a machine-speed alternative to a human bottleneck. Its parent problem, two connections, one lens, and sources follow.

The bluntest remedy for risky exploration is simply to ask a person first. Concrete Problems in AI Safety (2016) proposes exactly that, a human check on potentially unsafe actions, while conceding in the same breath that people are far too slow to review very many of them.

The prose walks through the proposal, the limit the paper states as it proposes it, and what replaces the human once the approach stops scaling. Beneath the sections sit the parent problem, one connection, one lens, and the source passages.

Before large language models, Weston and colleagues built the bAbI tasks: roughly twenty tiny question-answering puzzles, each isolating one skill a reading system ought to have. Concrete Problems in AI Safety (2016) points to them as a model for the diagnostic benchmark suite that safe exploration research still lacks.

A section on the benchmark suite itself comes first, then one explaining that the paper borrows its structure rather than its technique. The page closes with a single connection to safe exploration, the lens it sits in, and sources.

When the world a model faces drifts away from the world it trained on, one classical assumption offers a foothold: the inputs may change, but the relationship between input and label stays fixed. That is the covariate shift assumption, which Shimodaira formalized in 2000 and Concrete Problems in AI Safety (2016) inherits.

One section explains reweighting training data under a fixed conditional; a second explains why the paper treats the assumption warily. The concept's place under robustness to distributional shift, two connections, one lens, and sources come after.

Econometricians learned long ago to commit to only part of a model, assuming a few things about a distribution and staying agnostic about the rest. Partially specified models name that family of approaches, which Concrete Problems in AI Safety (2016) borrows as a way to survive distribution shift on weaker assumptions.

After a section on specifying only part of a distribution, the prose introduces a family with two children and one motivating retreat. The page then maps the parent problem and the two members this concept contains, three connections, its lens, and sources.

Hansen's generalized method of moments, from 1982, lets an econometrician pin down a model's parameters using only a handful of equations the true parameters must satisfy, no full description of the data's distribution required. It reaches this wiki as one of the partially specified approaches Concrete Problems in AI Safety (2016) surveys.

Identification from moment conditions alone occupies the first section; the second shows how the method generalizes the paper's founding example. The parent family, two connections, one lens, and links into the source close the page.

Can you tell how badly a model is failing on new data without any labels for that data? Unsupervised risk estimation, formalized in 2010 by Donmez, Lebanon, and Balasubramanian, answers yes, provided the model's error distribution has some assumed structure to lean on.

Estimating risk without labels comes first in the prose, followed by why this target is narrower than the ambitions of the rest of its family. The page then situates the concept under partially specified models and lists two connections, one lens, and the passages that cite it.

Practitioners have long hedged against surprise by training on several different distributions at once, wagering that a model performing well across all of them will cope with a genuinely new one. Concrete Problems in AI Safety (2016) records the habit as one of the plainer responses to distributional shift.

The prose treats the practice first as an engineering wager rather than a statistical assumption, then contrasts it with the covariate shift approach. A parent problem, a single connection, one lens, and source links sit beneath the sections.

What would have happened had the world been different? Statisticians and causal theorists from Neyman to Pearl built formal machinery for answering that question, and counterfactual reasoning is the umbrella this corpus gives it. Concrete Problems in AI Safety (2016) suggests it as a unifying way to think about distributional shift.

One section introduces the causal frameworks themselves; the next applies them as a lens on distributional shift. Below the prose, the page notes the parent problem, a single connection, the lens it appears under, and sources in the paper.

Software engineers write contracts: explicit promises about what a component will do, checkable at its interface. Carried into machine learning, the idea exposes an uncomfortable fact, that most ML systems rest on the brittle, unwritten promise that training and test data look alike.

The first section unpacks the borrowing from design-by-contract; the second shows how the reframing organizes three other concepts on this wiki. Afterward come the concept's place under robustness to distributional shift, the technique it contains, three connections, one lens, and sources.

Instead of retraining a faulty model, one line of work patches it. Model repair, due to Ghosh and colleagues in 2016, alters a trained model directly until a specified safety property holds, and it enters this corpus as a concrete instance of making machine learning honor a contract.

The sections cover patching versus retraining first, then the technique's role as the ex-post half of a pair. Closing blocks give the parent perspective, two connections, the two lenses this concept appears in, and deep links to the source.

Testing samples a system's behavior; formal verification proves it, mathematically, for every possible input. The approach has secured real safety-critical systems, most famously the federal aircraft collision avoidance system, and the AI-safety corpus keeps it in view as a standard that other methods rarely meet.

A section on proving rather than testing opens the prose, followed by one on the rigor Asimov's fictional law never received and modern machine learning still lacks. This concept stands outside any hierarchy here; a single connection, one lens, and sources complete the page.

A robot may not injure a human being. Asimov wrote his First Law as fiction in the 1940s, and half a century later Weld and Etzioni took it seriously enough to attempt a formalization within classical AI planning. This corpus remembers both moves.

The page tells that double story first, a fictional injunction and a serious attempt to formalize it, then explains why the corpus treats the law mainly as a foil. Two connections, the two lenses this concept sits in, and source links follow; it has no parent here.

Machine learning applied to sensitive records, medical data above all, raises a question of its own: what does a trained model give away about the people in its training set? Privacy research studies that leak, and Concrete Problems in AI Safety (2016) names it a neighbor to accident risk rather than a part of it.

First the prose covers what a model can reveal about its training data; then it explains why this hazard needs no adversary, unlike the field listed beside it. One connection, one lens, and sources end the page.

Whether machine learning systems discriminate, and how to keep them from doing so, is the business of fairness research. It appears in this corpus for a modest reason: Concrete Problems in AI Safety (2016) lists it among the related safety problems that fall outside its own study of accidents.

Three short sections follow: the field the paper deliberately sets aside, what that field actually studies, and why the paper places it outside accidents. With no recorded connections, the page closes on the boundary-drawing lens this concept belongs to and its sources.

What can a malicious adversary do to a legitimate machine learning system? That question defines security research, an established field Concrete Problems in AI Safety (2016) mentions precisely to set it outside its own scope, which concerns harms nobody intended.

The prose runs through three sections: an adjacent field defined by its adversary, the sense in which it mirrors accident risk one step removed, and the contrast with a neighboring field that needs no adversary at all. Two connections, one lens, and links to the cited lines follow.

An ML system can itself be the weapon, built or deployed to defraud, spam, or harm people at scale. That is what this corpus means by abuse, one of the adjacent research areas Concrete Problems in AI Safety (2016) gestures to while marking out its own territory of accidents.

A section on what the term covers comes first, then one on its modest place in the corpus. This page has no parent or children; a single connection to security research, the boundary-drawing lens, and sources sit at the bottom.

How can anyone understand what a complicated machine learning system is doing inside? Transparency research pursues that question, and Concrete Problems in AI Safety (2016) names the field in a single line, declining to develop it even though several of the paper's own proposals quietly assume it.

Three sections take this up: a field named in order to be set aside, the tool the paper's proposals often presuppose, and where the area sits relative to the rest. There are no connections to list; the lens and sources close the page.

The economic and social consequences of machine learning, for labor, industries, and governance, have a research area of their own. This corpus calls it policy, following Concrete Problems in AI Safety (2016), which mentions the field in one line while marking the edge of its own technical territory.

Two sections describe the adjacent field the paper declines to cover, then the boundary that brief mention draws. No connections are recorded for this concept, so the remaining blocks are the lens it shares with the paper's other exclusions and the source citation.

InstructGPT is what GPT-3 became after OpenAI taught it to follow instructions, through human demonstrations, human preference judgments, and reinforcement learning arranged as a three-step pipeline. Its 2022 paper found people preferred the tuned model's outputs even over those of a much larger untuned one.

The page runs through four sections: what InstructGPT is, the headline comparison showing the gains came from data rather than scale, where the model still falls short, and how it became the reference RLHF system downstream. One connection, one lens, and sources follow.

Underneath everything in the InstructGPT work sits GPT-3, the large autoregressive language model that Brown and colleagues introduced in 2020, trained to predict the next token across a vast sweep of text. Every model the paper trains, supervised, reward, or PPO, starts from it.

The prose explains what GPT-3 is, then its role in this corpus as the shared starting point, and finally a controlled comparison that teaches a lesson about where the improvements really came from. A single connection to InstructGPT, the pipeline lens, and source links round things out.

Take GPT-3, show it thousands of human-written demonstrations of good responses, and fine-tune on them directly: the result is the SFT model, the first trained artifact in the InstructGPT (2022) pipeline. It serves both as a baseline in its own right and as the seed for everything trained afterward.

From there the page moves through four sections: how the model is trained, an overfitting curve explained by the dataset's construction, its selection by the reward model it later initializes, and the way it quietly forks in two. Three connections, two lenses, and sources close the page.

Human judgment is expensive, so InstructGPT (2022) trained a stand-in: a model that reads a prompt and a response and returns a single score predicting which responses people would prefer. That reward model becomes the signal the rest of the pipeline optimizes against.

The prose asks first why the corpus needs a stand-in for human judgment, then what the model enabled downstream, and finally what it actually is. Beneath that, the page lists the three training details this concept contains, five connections, two lenses, and deep links into the papers that use it.

When a labeler ranks two model outputs, that preference becomes training signal through a pairwise loss: the gap between the rewards assigned to the preferred and dispreferred outputs is read as the log odds a human would favor the first. InstructGPT (2022) inherited the loss from earlier summarization work.

Three sections explain how the loss fits into the pipeline, walk through its mathematics, and draw out what its structure implies. The page then records its parent, the reward model itself, along with one connection, one lens, and the relevant source passages.

Ranking K outputs at once yields every pairwise comparison among them, and shuffling those correlated pairs into training as if they were independent makes a reward model overfit. The fix in InstructGPT (2022) is small: keep all the comparisons from one ranking inside a single batch element.

How the trick fits, what it enabled, and what it is, in that order, make up the page's three sections. The detail nests under the reward model; with no connections to show, the remaining blocks are its lens and sources.

Proximal Policy Optimization is the reinforcement learning algorithm behind the final step of the InstructGPT (2022) pipeline: starting from the supervised model, it nudges the policy toward outputs the reward model scores highly while limiting how far any single update can move.

Sections on the algorithm in general, its role as the third training stage, and its six working parts follow in that order. Those six parts reappear as the concepts this page contains, alongside two connections, the pipeline lens, and links into the paper.
